characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: precision extensometer developed by the authors, plus strain gages and a load cell
characterization_methods.key_findings: Young's modulus decreases with plastic strain, by more than 20% after 25% plastic strain (Fig. 1).
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Workpiece loaded to a maximum 25% plastic strain and unloaded; stress–strain curve monitored throughout
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure the elastic modulus of SPCE sheet metal before and after large plastic deformation
characterization_methods.technique: Precision tensile test with a precision extensometer and strain gages

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: Triboscope (Hysitron Inc.) mounted on an AFM stage SPM-9500J2 (Shimadzu Co.); spherical tip with nominal radius R = 50 μm; force range 1–10 mN (100 nN sensitivity), displacement range 5 μm (0.2 nm sensitivity)
characterization_methods.key_findings: The elastic modulus near the grain boundary has a smaller value than in other regions of the grain; the average values are smaller than the previous test because the real tip radius is smaller than the nominal value.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Indentation near a grain boundary (specimen labelled SPCE); nominal radius R = 50 μm; measurement grid with 1 μm interval, 20 points in X and 3 in Y; CMP treatment applied before indentation to avoid surface-roughness effects
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure the distribution of the elastic modulus (and hardness) within a grain, in particular near the grain boundary
characterization_methods.technique: Nano-indentation with a spherical indenter tip

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: SPM-9500J2 AFM stage (Shimadzu Co.) with 3D piezo stage controlled by an SPM controller
characterization_methods.key_findings: AFM height map shows a grain boundary as a dark diagonal band with three rows of indentation markers (Lines #1–#3) across it.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Surface profile scanned before and after indentation; position axis 0–12 μm
characterization_methods.purpose: Locate the grain boundary and the indentation points, and measure the surface profile in situ
characterization_methods.technique: Atomic force microscopy (AFM) imaging of the surface

characterization_methods.key_findings: Polycrystalline region with grains delimited by dark irregular boundaries and a few small dark inclusions/pores; targeted grain boundary identified under the microscope.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Surface of the specimen etched with an etching solution to disclose the grain boundary; measurement region marked as a rectangular area
characterization_methods.purpose: Reveal and locate the targeted grain boundary before nano-indentation (etching forms a several-nanometre ditch at the boundary)
characterization_methods.technique: Optical microscopy of an etched surface

characterization_methods.key_findings: Marker layout permits re-location of the measurement point after CMP (Fig. 10).
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Two indentation marks made near the targeted grain boundary; larger outer markers find the region, smaller inner markers fix the exact measurement point (marker spacings 300/340/300 μm)
characterization_methods.purpose: Mark the exact position so the targeted grain boundary can be relocated after CMP treatment
characterization_methods.technique: Vickers hardness indentation for location marking

analytical_models.equation_role: describes the decrease of the elastic modulus with true (plastic) strain measured by the precision extensometer
analytical_models.model_name: Quadratic fit of elastic modulus vs true strain
analytical_models.model_note: E = E0*(351ε² − 160ε + 93.8), as annotated on Fig. 1.

computational_details.boundary_and_initial_conditions: V-bending test; the elastic modulus was set either to the constant initial value or to the strain-dependent (varied) modulus taken from the experimental results of Fig. 1
computational_details.simulation_method: Finite-element (FEM) simulation of spring-back after V-bending
computational_details.software_used: an FEM code (not named in the paper)
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: Spring-back computed with the varied elastic modulus could be predicted more accurately than with the constant initial elastic modulus when compared with the experimental spring-back (Fig. 2).

defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: Dislocations released from a common source move along the same slip surface and pile up; the front of the dislocations is stopped by obstacles such as grain boundaries and solutes. The piled-up dislocations can move backwards when the shearing stress is released during unloading, which lowers the apparent elastic modulus; the decrease increases as a function of the plastic strain.

interfaces.interface_notes: The pile-up model (Fig. 3) is qualitative (no magnitudes printed); near the boundary the apparent elastic modulus is locally lower than in the grain interior.
interfaces.slip_behavior: Dislocations move along the same slip surface and pile up at the grain boundary; the pile-up configuration gives a movable-dislocation population that deforms even at stresses below the yield stress.

comparative_performance.comparison_metric: Experimental V-bending spring-back (rising from a little above 0.8° to just under 1.4° as bend angle falls from 160° to 90°) compared with FE simulations using the constant initial elastic modulus (lowest, ~1.0° to ~1.2°) and using the strain-dependent varied modulus (tracks the experimental points closely)

lifetime_prediction.model_used: FEM simulation of spring-back after V-bending

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: SPCE sheet metal workpiece was loaded in tension to a given plastic strain of maximum 25% during the precision tensile test using a precision extensometer and strain gages.
The workpiece was unloaded after reaching the maximum 25% plastic strain; the elastic modulus was then measured from the unloading curve after the given plastic deformation.

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Precision tensile test using the authors' precision extensometer and strain gages; the workpiece was loaded to a maximum plastic strain of 25% and then unloaded; elastic modulus measured from the stress–strain curve at initial elastic deformation and from the unloading curve after plastic deformation.

youngs_modulus.value: variation δE = E/E0 decreases from 100% (undeformed reference) to ≈75% at true strain ≈0.25–0.27; i.e. the modulus decreases by more than 20% after a deformation of 25% plastic strain

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Nano-indentation with a spherical indenter tip (nominal radius R = 50 μm) along lines across a grain boundary; measurement grid with 1 μm interval and 20 × 3 points in X and Y.
measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: SPCE specimen (Fig. 10 specimen outline labelled 'SPCE'), grain-boundary region

youngs_modulus.value: compound/indentation elastic modulus Er near the grain boundary is lower than in the interior; most values scatter between ≈150 and ≈400 GPa, with the lowest point next to the boundary falling to ≈50 GPa (values read from the scatter plots)

grain_structure.texture: grains at different orientations give different measured modulus levels.

phases_present.phase_name: Fe matrix (mild steel, C dissolved in Fe)

microstructure_list.region: grain interior (away from the grain boundary)

structures.overall_structure: Polycrystalline SPCE (mild steel) sheet containing grains separated by grain boundaries; after large plastic deformation the dislocation structure changes so that movable dislocations and dislocation pile-up near grain boundaries govern the (reduced) apparent elastic modulus.

unmapped_findings: The nano-indentation (microscopic) specimens are labelled only as SPCE in Fig. 10; the text does not restate that they were tested specifically after the 25% tensile deformation, so the near-grain-boundary modulus reduction (Figs. 9 and 12) cannot be unambiguously tied to the as-deformed (after-25%) state rather than to the general SPCE material.

A post-tensile-test heat treatment of 373 K for 90 h was applied to some workpieces to recover only the Cottrell atmosphere (diffusion of C in the Fe matrix) while keeping dislocations stationary; the condition was calculated from the average diffusion distance X = (2Dt)^(1/2). This defines a separate heat-treated condition, not the as-deformed after-25% sample.

Table 1 (specimens A–E: as received, with 15% pre-strain, heat-treated after 15% pre-strain, heat-treated after received, annealed), Table 2, and Fig. 4 concern a different material, SPCC sheet of 1.2 mm thickness with 15% pre-strain, and are excluded from the SPCE after-25%-deformation sample.

The paper attributes the decrease of the elastic modulus after plastic deformation to three reasons: increase of residual stress (which disturbs elastic recovery), increase of micro-cracks (which decrease density; the density reduction due to plastic deformation is less than 1%), and variation in the dislocation structure (movable/piled-up dislocations).

In mild steel, dislocations may be locked by carbon and other solutes (Cottrell effect) before plastic deformation; during plastic deformation they are released and move with lower internal stress, and the Cottrell atmosphere is not recovered at room temperature because the diffusion rate of C in the Fe matrix is very low.
